---
title: "03.1-eDNA: a simple eDNA metabarcoding workflow"
editor: visual
---

## What this page does

This page takes raw eDNA sequencing reads and turns them into a table of which organisms were found in each sample. It is meant as a reference for ecologists who are new to bioinformatics: every step is one command (or a short loop), and the text explains what it does and why.

**The data.** eDNA samples from two sites at Yellow Island (Site 1 and Site 5). DNA from each sample was amplified by PCR with primers for two "barcode" genes, and the two products were sequenced together on an Illumina NextSeq 2000 (paired-end, 2 × 301 bp):

| Marker | What it detects | Forward primer | Reverse primer |
|--------|-----------------|----------------|----------------|
| 18S V9 | Most eukaryotes (algae, protists, animals, fungi) | `GTACACACCGCCCGTC` | `TGATCCTTCTGCAGGTTCACCTAC` |
| COI (Leray) | Mostly animals | `GGWACWGGWTGAACWGTWTAYCCYCC` | `TANACYTCNGGRTGNCCRAARAAYCA` |

Letters like `W`, `Y` and `N` in the primers are "wildcards" that match more than one base (e.g. `W` = A or T, `N` = any base).

**The workflow.**

1.  Download the reads
2.  Import the reads into QIIME 2
3.  Look at read quality
4.  Remove primers and split the reads by marker
5.  Denoise with DADA2 to get ASVs (exact sequences) and a count table
6.  Download reference databases
7.  Assign taxonomy to each ASV
8.  Make bar plots
9.  Compare diversity between sites

Almost everything after the download runs in **QIIME 2**, a widely used program for amplicon (barcode) data.

**How to run it.** Run the chunks in order, from top to bottom. All paths are relative to the `code/` folder. Results go to `../output/03.1-eDNA/`.

**Viewing results.** QIIME 2 saves data as `.qza` files and reports as `.qzv` files. To look at a `.qzv`, drag it onto <https://view.qiime2.org>.

## 1. Download the reads

`wget` downloads every read file (`.fastq.gz`) and its checksum file (`.md5`) from the lab server. `-nc` skips files you already have, so you can rerun this if the download stops partway.

```{bash}
mkdir -p ../data/raw/eDNA-yellow_island-2023
cd ../data/raw/eDNA-yellow_island-2023

wget -r -np -nd -nc -A "*.fastq.gz,*.md5" \
  https://owl.fish.washington.edu/nightingales/eDNA-yellow_island-2023/
```

A checksum is a fingerprint of a file. If a downloaded file's checksum matches the one from the server, the file arrived intact. This prints any file that does **not** match; no output means everything is fine.

```{bash}
cd ../data/raw/eDNA-yellow_island-2023
cat *.md5 | md5sum -c --quiet
```

## 2. Import the reads into QIIME 2

QIIME 2 needs a **manifest**: a table listing each sample and where its two read files (R1 and R2) are. This loop writes one row per sample. It skips samples whose files are empty or that are missing R2 (`Site5t_S125`), since QIIME 2 can't import those. It also skips two samples with almost no reads: `Site5J_S107` (70 read pairs) and `Site5w_S128` (13 read pairs). Samples this small give too few reads after filtering to say anything about the community.

It also writes a **sample metadata** file, which records information about each sample. Here that is just the site (`Site1` or `Site5`), taken from the sample name. You can add more columns later (date, depth, replicate, ...).

```{bash}
mkdir -p ../output/03.1-eDNA
cd ../output/03.1-eDNA

raw=$(realpath ../../data/raw/eDNA-yellow_island-2023)

printf "sample-id\tforward-absolute-filepath\treverse-absolute-filepath\n" > manifest.tsv
printf "sample-id\tsite\n" > sample-metadata.tsv

for r1 in ${raw}/*_R1_001.fastq.gz; do
  r2=${r1/_R1_/_R2_}
  sample=$(basename "$r1" _R1_001.fastq.gz)   # e.g. Yell_July18_Site1a_S83
  sample=${sample#Yell_July18_}                # e.g. Site1a_S83
  site=${sample:0:5}                           # e.g. Site1

  # skip samples with no R2 file or no reads
  if [ ! -f "$r2" ] || [ -z "$(zcat "$r1" | head -c 1)" ]; then
    echo "Skipping $sample"
    continue
  fi

  # skip samples with too few reads to use
  if [ "$sample" = "Site5J_S107" ] || [ "$sample" = "Site5w_S128" ]; then
    echo "Skipping $sample (too few reads)"
    continue
  fi

  printf "%s\t%s\t%s\n" "$sample" "$r1" "$r2" >> manifest.tsv
  printf "%s\t%s\n" "$sample" "$site" >> sample-metadata.tsv
done
```

Now import the reads. Every QIIME 2 chunk starts by turning on ("activating") the QIIME 2 software environment, because Quarto runs each chunk in a fresh shell.

```{bash}
source /opt/anaconda/anaconda3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh
conda activate qiime2-2026.7
cd ../output/03.1-eDNA

qiime tools import \
  --type 'SampleData[PairedEndSequencesWithQuality]' \
  --input-path manifest.tsv \
  --input-format PairedEndFastqManifestPhred33V2 \
  --output-path demux.qza
```

## 3. Look at read quality

This makes a report (`demux.qzv`) with the number of reads per sample and a plot of base quality along the reads. Quality usually drops toward the end of the reads, especially R2. Samples with very few reads (a few hundred or less) won't give useful results.

```{bash}
source /opt/anaconda/anaconda3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh
conda activate qiime2-2026.7
cd ../output/03.1-eDNA

qiime demux summarize \
  --i-data demux.qza \
  --o-visualization demux.qzv
```

## 4. Remove primers and split by marker

Each sample contains reads from both markers mixed together. `cutadapt` is run twice: once looking for the 18S V9 primers and once for the COI primers. Each run keeps only the reads that start with that marker's primers and cuts the primers off, so we end up with one set of reads per marker.

-   `--p-front-f` / `--p-front-r`: the primer at the start of R1 / R2. `^` means the primer must be at the very start of the read. The part after `...` is the *other* primer, written in reverse complement. It's only found when a read runs all the way through a short DNA fragment, and it's cut off along with everything after it (adapter and junk). `;optional` means reads are kept whether or not this second primer is found
-   `--p-discard-untrimmed`: throw away reads without the primers (i.e. reads from the other marker)
-   `--p-nextseq-trim 20`: trim low-quality bases from the end of reads. The NextSeq reads "no signal" as a run of G's with high quality scores, and this option handles that correctly
-   `--p-minimum-length 50`: drop reads shorter than 50 bases after trimming

**18S V9:**

```{bash}
source /opt/anaconda/anaconda3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh
conda activate qiime2-2026.7
cd ../output/03.1-eDNA

qiime cutadapt trim-paired \
  --i-demultiplexed-sequences demux.qza \
  --p-front-f "^GTACACACCGCCCGTC...GTAGGTGAACCTGCAGAAGGATCA;optional" \
  --p-front-r "^TGATCCTTCTGCAGGTTCACCTAC...GACGGGCGGTGTGTAC;optional" \
  --p-discard-untrimmed \
  --p-nextseq-trim 20 \
  --p-minimum-length 50 \
  --p-cores 8 \
  --o-trimmed-sequences V9-demux.qza \
  --o-stats V9-cutadapt-stats.qza
```

**COI:**

```{bash}
source /opt/anaconda/anaconda3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh
conda activate qiime2-2026.7
cd ../output/03.1-eDNA

qiime cutadapt trim-paired \
  --i-demultiplexed-sequences demux.qza \
  --p-front-f "^GGWACWGGWTGAACWGTWTAYCCYCC...TGRTTYTTYGGNCAYCCNGARGTNTA;optional" \
  --p-front-r "^TANACYTCNGGRTGNCCRAARAAYCA...GGRGGRTAWACWGTTCAWCCWGTWCC;optional" \
  --p-discard-untrimmed \
  --p-nextseq-trim 20 \
  --p-minimum-length 50 \
  --p-cores 8 \
  --o-trimmed-sequences COI-demux.qza \
  --o-stats COI-cutadapt-stats.qza
```

To see what share of each sample's reads belonged to each marker, make a table from the stats (`percent-reads-after` column):

```{bash}
source /opt/anaconda/anaconda3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh
conda activate qiime2-2026.7
cd ../output/03.1-eDNA

for marker in V9 COI; do
  qiime metadata tabulate \
    --m-input-file ${marker}-cutadapt-stats.qza \
    --o-visualization ${marker}-cutadapt-stats.qzv
done
```

## 5. Denoise with DADA2

Sequencing makes small errors, so one real DNA sequence shows up as many slightly different reads. **DADA2** learns the error pattern of this sequencing run and uses it to work out the real sequences. It also:

-   filters out low-quality reads
-   merges each R1/R2 pair into one sequence
-   removes chimeras (fake sequences made of two different organisms, created during PCR)

The result is a list of **ASVs** (amplicon sequence variants: exact, error-corrected sequences) and a **feature table** with the number of reads of each ASV in each sample. This step is the slowest; expect it to take a while.

`--p-trunc-len-f` / `--p-trunc-len-r` cut R1 / R2 to a fixed length to remove their low-quality ends. Reads shorter than that length are dropped. `0` means "don't cut".

**18S V9.** The V9 region (about 90–190 bp) is shorter than the reads, so cutadapt has already trimmed each read to the right length. No further cutting is needed.

```{bash}
source /opt/anaconda/anaconda3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh
conda activate qiime2-2026.7
cd ../output/03.1-eDNA

qiime dada2 denoise-paired \
  --i-demultiplexed-seqs V9-demux.qza \
  --p-trunc-len-f 0 \
  --p-trunc-len-r 0 \
  --p-n-threads 16 \
  --o-table V9-table.qza \
  --o-representative-sequences V9-rep-seqs.qza \
  --o-denoising-stats V9-dada2-stats.qza \
  --o-base-transition-stats V9-dada2-error-model.qza
```

**COI.** The COI region is about 313 bp, longer than either read, so R1 and R2 only overlap near their ends, which is where quality is lowest. Cutting R1 to 200 bp and R2 to 180 bp removes the worst bases and still leaves about 67 bp of overlap for merging (200 + 180 − 313). In a test with three samples, this kept 52–65% of COI reads, compared with 23–32% without cutting.

```{bash}
source /opt/anaconda/anaconda3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh
conda activate qiime2-2026.7
cd ../output/03.1-eDNA

qiime dada2 denoise-paired \
  --i-demultiplexed-seqs COI-demux.qza \
  --p-trunc-len-f 200 \
  --p-trunc-len-r 180 \
  --p-n-threads 16 \
  --o-table COI-table.qza \
  --o-representative-sequences COI-rep-seqs.qza \
  --o-denoising-stats COI-dada2-stats.qza \
  --o-base-transition-stats COI-dada2-error-model.qza
```

Check how many reads made it through each DADA2 step (`*-dada2-stats.qzv`). If most reads are lost at "filtered", the truncation lengths are too long; if most are lost at "merged", they are too short (R1 and R2 no longer overlap). `*-table.qzv` shows reads and ASVs per sample.

```{bash}
source /opt/anaconda/anaconda3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh
conda activate qiime2-2026.7
cd ../output/03.1-eDNA

for marker in V9 COI; do
  qiime metadata tabulate \
    --m-input-file ${marker}-dada2-stats.qza \
    --o-visualization ${marker}-dada2-stats.qzv

  qiime feature-table summarize \
    --i-table ${marker}-table.qza \
    --m-metadata-file sample-metadata.tsv \
    --o-feature-frequencies ${marker}-feature-frequencies.qza \
    --o-sample-frequencies ${marker}-sample-frequencies.qza \
    --o-summary ${marker}-table.qzv
done
```

## 6. Download reference databases

To name the organism behind each ASV, we compare it to a **reference database** of DNA sequences from known species.

The databases are saved in `../data/reference/` so they can be reused by other projects. You only need to run these chunks once.

**18S V9: PR2.** PR2 is a curated database of 18S rRNA sequences from protists and other eukaryotes. QIIME 2's `rescript` plugin downloads it and converts it to QIIME 2 format in one step.

```{bash}
source /opt/anaconda/anaconda3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh
conda activate qiime2-2026.7
mkdir -p ../data/reference
cd ../data/reference

qiime rescript get-pr2-data \
  --o-pr2-sequences pr2-seqs.qza \
  --o-pr2-taxonomy pr2-taxonomy.qza
```

**COI: MIDORI2.** MIDORI2 is a database of mitochondrial gene sequences from GenBank. Its files are archived on Zenodo (<https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22685700>). This chunk:

1.  downloads the QIIME-format release (433 MB; it has files for all mitochondrial genes)
2.  unzips just the two COI files (`CO1`): the sequences and their taxonomy
3.  checks them against the checksums published with the release (it should print `OK` twice)

```{bash}
mkdir -p ../data/reference
cd ../data/reference

zenodo=https://zenodo.org/api/records/22685701/files

curl -L -o MIDORI2_GB273_QIIME.zip ${zenodo}/MIDORI2_GB273_QIIME.zip/content
curl -L -o MIDORI2_GB273_sha256.txt ${zenodo}/release_sha256.txt/content

unzip -o MIDORI2_GB273_QIIME.zip \
  QIIME/uniq/MIDORI2_UNIQ_NUC_GB273_CO1_QIIME.fasta.gz \
  QIIME/uniq/MIDORI2_UNIQ_NUC_GB273_CO1_QIIME.taxon.gz

grep "UNIQ_NUC_GB273_CO1_QIIME" MIDORI2_GB273_sha256.txt | sha256sum -c
```

Next, import the COI files into QIIME 2. Two small fixes are needed first:

-   QIIME 2 can't read the compressed (`.gz`) sequence file, so `zcat` uncompresses it
-   MIDORI2 adds an NCBI ID number to every name (e.g. `p__Arthropoda_6656`). The `sed` command removes these numbers so the names are easier to read in plots

```{bash}
source /opt/anaconda/anaconda3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh
conda activate qiime2-2026.7
cd ../data/reference

zcat QIIME/uniq/MIDORI2_UNIQ_NUC_GB273_CO1_QIIME.fasta.gz > midori2-CO1-seqs.fasta

zcat QIIME/uniq/MIDORI2_UNIQ_NUC_GB273_CO1_QIIME.taxon.gz \
  | sed -E 's/_[0-9]+(;|$)/\1/g' > midori2-CO1-taxonomy.tsv

qiime tools import \
  --type 'FeatureData[Sequence]' \
  --input-path midori2-CO1-seqs.fasta \
  --output-path midori2-CO1-seqs.qza

qiime tools import \
  --type 'FeatureData[Taxonomy]' \
  --input-format HeaderlessTSVTaxonomyFormat \
  --input-path midori2-CO1-taxonomy.tsv \
  --output-path midori2-CO1-taxonomy.qza
```

## 7. Assign taxonomy

Each ASV is compared to the reference database with `vsearch`. For each ASV, vsearch finds up to 10 reference sequences that are at least a set percent identical. The ASV gets the part of their names that most of them agree on (a "consensus"). For example, if the hits are all copepods but different species, the ASV is named only down to "Copepoda". ASVs with no good hits are labeled `Unassigned`.

-   `--p-perc-identity`: how similar a reference must be to count as a hit. 18S V9 uses 0.9 (90%). COI uses 0.8 (80%), because many marine invertebrates have no COI sequence in GenBank. In a test, 90% left about 80% of COI reads unassigned, while 80% left about 33% unassigned
-   `--p-maxrejects 100`: stop searching after 100 references that don't match. Without this, vsearch checks every reference sequence, which is several times slower with almost the same result
-   `--p-threads 16`: use 16 CPU cores
-   Outputs: `*-taxonomy.qza` (the name for each ASV) and `*-vsearch-hits.qza` (the reference hits each name is based on)

**18S V9:**

```{bash}
source /opt/anaconda/anaconda3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh
conda activate qiime2-2026.7
cd ../output/03.1-eDNA

qiime feature-classifier classify-consensus-vsearch \
  --i-query V9-rep-seqs.qza \
  --i-reference-reads ../../data/reference/pr2-seqs.qza \
  --i-reference-taxonomy ../../data/reference/pr2-taxonomy.qza \
  --p-perc-identity 0.9 \
  --p-maxrejects 100 \
  --p-threads 16 \
  --o-classification V9-taxonomy.qza \
  --o-search-results V9-vsearch-hits.qza
```

**COI:**

```{bash}
source /opt/anaconda/anaconda3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh
conda activate qiime2-2026.7
cd ../output/03.1-eDNA

qiime feature-classifier classify-consensus-vsearch \
  --i-query COI-rep-seqs.qza \
  --i-reference-reads ../../data/reference/midori2-CO1-seqs.qza \
  --i-reference-taxonomy ../../data/reference/midori2-CO1-taxonomy.qza \
  --p-perc-identity 0.8 \
  --p-maxrejects 100 \
  --p-threads 16 \
  --o-classification COI-taxonomy.qza \
  --o-search-results COI-vsearch-hits.qza
```

Treat names below the family level with caution, especially for COI at 80% identity: a hit at that level means "related to", not "the same species".

## 8. Make bar plots

A taxa bar plot shows, for each sample, what share of reads came from each group of organisms. In the viewer you can choose the taxonomic level (phylum, class, ...) and sort or group samples by site.

```{bash}
source /opt/anaconda/anaconda3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh
conda activate qiime2-2026.7
cd ../output/03.1-eDNA

for marker in V9 COI; do
  qiime taxa barplot \
    --i-table ${marker}-table.qza \
    --i-taxonomy ${marker}-taxonomy.qza \
    --m-metadata-file sample-metadata.tsv \
    --o-visualization ${marker}-taxa-barplot.qzv
done
```

## 9. Compare diversity between sites

This step asks two questions for each marker:

-   **Alpha diversity:** does one site have more kinds of organisms per sample than the other?
-   **Beta diversity:** are the communities at the two sites different in which organisms they contain?

### Remove reads that couldn't be named

Reads from ASVs labeled `Unassigned` (and, for 18S, reads from bacteria, which the 18S primers sometimes pick up) are removed first, so the comparison is about eukaryotes we could identify.

-   `--p-include "d__Eukaryota"`: for 18S V9, keep only ASVs whose name contains `d__Eukaryota` (PR2's label for eukaryotes)
-   `--p-exclude "Unassigned"`: for COI, remove ASVs labeled `Unassigned`

The `summarize` command then shows how many reads each sample has left, which is needed for the next step.

```{bash}
source /opt/anaconda/anaconda3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh
conda activate qiime2-2026.7
cd ../output/03.1-eDNA

qiime taxa filter-table \
  --i-table V9-table.qza \
  --i-taxonomy V9-taxonomy.qza \
  --p-include "d__Eukaryota" \
  --o-filtered-table V9-table-filtered.qza

qiime taxa filter-table \
  --i-table COI-table.qza \
  --i-taxonomy COI-taxonomy.qza \
  --p-exclude "Unassigned" \
  --o-filtered-table COI-table-filtered.qza

for marker in V9 COI; do
  qiime feature-table summarize \
    --i-table ${marker}-table-filtered.qza \
    --m-metadata-file sample-metadata.tsv \
    --o-feature-frequencies ${marker}-filtered-feature-frequencies.qza \
    --o-sample-frequencies ${marker}-filtered-sample-frequencies.qza \
    --o-summary ${marker}-table-filtered.qzv
done
```

COI has many diatom reads (about a third in this data set), because the Leray primers also amplify diatoms. To study only animals, you could also filter the COI table to animal phyla (e.g. `--p-include "p__Arthropoda,p__Annelida,p__Mollusca,p__Cnidaria"`).

### Choose a rarefaction depth

Samples have very different numbers of reads, and a sample with more reads will show more ASVs just because more of it was sampled. **Rarefaction** fixes this by randomly subsampling every sample down to the same number of reads (the **sampling depth**). Samples with fewer reads than the depth are left out.

Choosing the depth is a trade-off: a higher depth captures more of each community but drops more samples. Rarefaction curves help. They show how many ASVs are found as more reads are sampled; where a curve levels off, extra reads add few new ASVs.

-   `--p-max-depth`: the largest depth to plot. Choose about the read count of a typical sample (see `*-table-filtered.qzv`)
-   `--p-metrics observed_features`: plot the number of ASVs

```{bash}
source /opt/anaconda/anaconda3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh
conda activate qiime2-2026.7
cd ../output/03.1-eDNA

qiime diversity alpha-rarefaction \
  --i-table V9-table-filtered.qza \
  --p-max-depth 30000 \
  --p-metrics observed_features \
  --m-metadata-file sample-metadata.tsv \
  --o-visualization V9-alpha-rarefaction.qzv

qiime diversity alpha-rarefaction \
  --i-table COI-table-filtered.qza \
  --p-max-depth 6000 \
  --p-metrics observed_features \
  --m-metadata-file sample-metadata.tsv \
  --o-visualization COI-alpha-rarefaction.qzv
```

The depths used here:

-   **18S V9: 15,000 reads.** The curves are close to level by this depth. Five samples have fewer reads and are left out (`Site5g`, `Site1J`, `Site1U`, `Site5q`, `Site5f`; most of their reads were COI), leaving 46 samples (25 from Site 1, 21 from Site 5)
-   **COI: 2,000 reads.** Three samples have fewer reads and are left out (`Site5h`, `Site5f`, `Site1f`; most of their reads were 18S), leaving 49 samples (27 from Site 1, 22 from Site 5). The COI curves are still rising at 2,000, so richness is underestimated. Comparisons between sites are still fair, since every sample is subsampled to the same depth. A higher depth would drop more samples

If you rerun this with new data, check the two `.qzv` files and change the depths in the next chunk.

### Calculate diversity

`core-metrics` rarefies the table to the sampling depth and calculates the standard diversity measures in one step. All results go into one folder per marker (`--output-dir`).

-   **Alpha diversity** (one number per sample): `observed_features` (number of ASVs), `shannon` (combines the number of ASVs and how evenly reads are spread among them) and `evenness`
-   **Beta diversity** (one number per pair of samples, saved as a distance matrix): `bray_curtis` (differences in which ASVs are present *and* how abundant they are) and `jaccard` (only which ASVs are present)
-   **PCoA plots** (`*_emperor.qzv`): a 3D plot where each point is a sample, and samples with similar communities are close together. Color the points by `site` in the viewer
-   `--p-random-seed 42`: rarefaction subsamples at random; fixing the seed makes the result the same every time the chunk is run

```{bash}
source /opt/anaconda/anaconda3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh
conda activate qiime2-2026.7
cd ../output/03.1-eDNA

qiime diversity core-metrics \
  --i-table V9-table-filtered.qza \
  --p-sampling-depth 15000 \
  --m-metadata-file sample-metadata.tsv \
  --p-random-seed 42 \
  --output-dir V9-core-metrics

qiime diversity core-metrics \
  --i-table COI-table-filtered.qza \
  --p-sampling-depth 2000 \
  --m-metadata-file sample-metadata.tsv \
  --p-random-seed 42 \
  --output-dir COI-core-metrics
```

`--output-dir` stops with an error if the folder already exists. To rerun this chunk, delete the `V9-core-metrics` and `COI-core-metrics` folders first.

### Test for differences between sites

-   `alpha-group-significance` compares alpha diversity between sites with a **Kruskal-Wallis test** (a rank-based test that doesn't assume the data are normally distributed). It makes a box plot for each site
-   `beta-group-significance` tests whether communities differ between sites with **PERMANOVA**, using the Bray-Curtis distances. It asks whether samples from the same site are more similar to each other than to samples from the other site
    -   `--m-metadata-column site`: the column in `sample-metadata.tsv` that defines the groups

```{bash}
source /opt/anaconda/anaconda3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh
conda activate qiime2-2026.7
cd ../output/03.1-eDNA

for marker in V9 COI; do
  for metric in shannon observed_features; do
    qiime diversity alpha-group-significance \
      --i-alpha-diversity ${marker}-core-metrics/${metric}_vector.qza \
      --m-metadata-file sample-metadata.tsv \
      --o-visualization ${marker}-${metric}-by-site.qzv
  done

  qiime diversity beta-group-significance \
    --i-distance-matrix ${marker}-core-metrics/bray_curtis_distance_matrix.qza \
    --m-metadata-file sample-metadata.tsv \
    --m-metadata-column site \
    --o-visualization ${marker}-bray-curtis-by-site.qzv
done
```

**Results from this run:**

| Marker | Measure | Site 1 (median) | Site 5 (median) | p-value |
|--------|---------|-----------------|-----------------|---------|
| 18S V9 | Shannon diversity | 6.0 | 5.3 | < 0.001 |
| 18S V9 | Number of ASVs | 497 | 361 | 0.04 |
| 18S V9 | Community composition (Bray-Curtis PERMANOVA) | | | 0.001 |
| COI | Shannon diversity | 4.8 | 5.4 | 0.08 |
| COI | Number of ASVs | 152 | 178 | 0.17 |
| COI | Community composition (Bray-Curtis PERMANOVA) | | | 0.001 |

Site 1 has more diverse eukaryote communities by 18S, but COI shows no clear difference in alpha diversity. Both markers show that the two sites have different communities (PERMANOVA). A significant PERMANOVA can also mean the sites differ in how *variable* their samples are, not only in their average community; `qiime diversity beta-group-significance --p-method permdisp` tests for that.

## Glossary

-   **Alpha diversity**: diversity within one sample, e.g. the number of ASVs or the Shannon index
-   **Amplicon**: a piece of DNA copied many times by PCR. Here, the 18S V9 or COI barcode region
-   **ASV (amplicon sequence variant)**: an exact DNA sequence that DADA2 concludes is real (not a sequencing error). Roughly, one ASV ≈ one species or strain
-   **Beta diversity**: how different two samples' communities are. Bray-Curtis and Jaccard are two ways to measure it (0 = identical, 1 = nothing shared)
-   **Chimera**: a fake sequence formed during PCR from two different organisms' DNA
-   **Feature table**: a table of read counts, with ASVs as rows and samples as columns
-   **FASTQ**: the file format for sequencing reads: each read's DNA sequence plus a quality score for each base
-   **Paired-end (R1 / R2)**: each DNA fragment is read from both ends. R1 is the forward read and R2 the reverse read
-   **PERMANOVA**: a test of whether groups of samples (here, sites) have different communities, based on a distance matrix
-   **Primer**: a short DNA sequence that starts PCR copying at a specific place in the genome
-   **Rarefaction**: randomly subsampling every sample to the same number of reads, so samples with more reads don't look more diverse just because of sequencing effort
-   **Reverse complement**: the sequence of the opposite DNA strand, read in the same direction (A↔T, C↔G, reversed)
